Club overview

Level: B1+/B2, Adults

Time: 60-75

Dialect: American

Goal: can discuss financial secrets, compare ways of managing money, and express opinions about financial decisions in relationships

Ученику скрыта

(скрытая для учителя) Sensitive-topic guidance

Consider avoiding questions about students’ actual salaries, debts or personal relationships, as these topics may be sensitive. Fictional scenarios can work just as well for discussion. It may also help to acknowledge that couples manage money in different ways, and that financial privacy and honesty can coexist.

Love, Lies & Money: When Does Privacy Become a Secret?
They say love is built on trust. But what happens when your partner trusts you with their heart... but not their credit card bill?

Imagine discovering that your partner has a secret bank account. Would you feel angry, hurt, or completely fine with it? Many couples disagree about how much money information they should share. Some choose to have a joint bank account and share expenses, while others prefer to keep their finances separate and be financially independent. But where do we draw the line between privacy and keeping secrets?

According to a 2026 Bankrate survey, 45% of Americans who are married or living with a partner don't know everything about each other's finances. Even more surprisingly, 43% of U.S. adults believe that hiding financial secrets is just as bad as, or worse than, cheating on a partner. Apparently, money secrets are a pretty serious business!

But does having a separate bank account automatically mean you're hiding something? If both partners have agreed to keep some money separate, that might be perfectly fine. But secretly borrowing thousands of dollars while planning to buy a house together? That's a different story. Keeping something important from your partner can break their trust, especially when your decisions affect both of you.

So why do people keep financial secrets? According to the same survey, among Americans who don't share all their financial information with their partners, 28% say they believe they have the right to keep some things private, while 14% say they would feel embarrassed if their partner knew. Others may simply find it difficult to bring up a sensitive topic like debt or spending habits.

Money can also mean different things to different people. For one partner, saving money means feeling safe. For another, spending money on travel and experiences means enjoying life. These differences can lead to arguments, even when both people have good reasons for their choices.

In the end, maybe the secret to a healthy relationship isn't sharing every dollar. It's agreeing on what can stay private and what needs to be discussed openly. After all, you can share a future without sharing a bank account. But can you share a future without sharing the truth?
Source: https://www.bankrate.com/press-releases/43-believe-financial-infidelity-is-at-least-as-bad-as-physical-cheating/

Useful phrases:

  • I didn't mention it because…

  • The reason I didn't tell you was that...

  • What bothers me most is..

Ученику скрыта

Possible answers

Case A:

Possible reasons:

  • Alex thought they could replace the money before the vacation.
  • Alex believed they could spend their own money without asking for permission.
  • Alex was afraid Jordan would disapprove of the purchase.
  • Alex had wanted the gaming setup for a long time and made an impulsive decision.

Possible reactions:

  • Jordan feels hurt because Alex kept the purchase a secret.
  • Jordan is disappointed that their vacation plans might have to change.
  • Jordan worries that Alex might hide other expensive purchases in the future.

Case B:

Possible reasons:

  • Taylor feels embarrassed about having so much debt.
  • Taylor is afraid Morgan will reconsider moving in together.
  • Taylor hoped to pay off the debt before Morgan found out.

Possible reactions:

  • Morgan feels disappointed that Taylor didn't share such important information.
  • Morgan worries that the debt could affect their ability to pay rent.

Student C: Explain the new model and add another name.

Money models in a relationship:

1. Income-based split
Both partners contribute to shared expenses based on their income. The partner who earns more pays a larger share.

2. One money manager
One partner manages all the bills and savings, but both partners can access their money and make important decisions together. / One partner controls all the money. The other partner must ask for money and explain why they need it.

Ученику скрыта

Possible answers

Everything equal
Both partners pay exactly half of all shared expenses, even if one earns much more than the other.

The category split
Each partner is responsible for different expenses. For example, one pays the rent while the other pays for groceries and utilities.

Taking turns
Partners take turns paying for certain expenses. For example, one pays for dates this month, and the other pays next month.

Separate finances
Both partners keep their own money and agree on how to split shared expenses. They don't have a joint bank account.

Yours, mine & ours
Both partners keep their own accounts but also put money into a shared account for bills and joint plans.

One pays, one saves
One partner pays for everyday expenses, while the other saves money for their shared future.

Ученику скрыта

TN

Put students in pairs in breakout rooms.

If students feel comfortable, invite them to share which money models they've seen in their own families or among people they know. Remind everyone to respect different approaches and avoid judging others. Sharing personal experiences is optional.

⏱️ Suggested timing: 7–9 minutes.

Support for less confident students:
If students haven't written down enough money models in 1.1, reveal the Possible Answers from that task. Let them use the list as a reference during the discussion.
